and proceed step-by-step (G1) and perform actions and get feedback on the actions they perform on each step (G3).

structure.title: CoCapture: Effectively Communicating UI Behaviors on Existing Websites by Demonstrating and Remixing

figure_descriptions.alt:
Figure 1: The workflow of CoCapture. There are four steps of using CoCapture to communicate new UI behavior mockups
on an existing website. (Step 1) Users first capture existing interface behaviors (base scene) by interacting with the website
(scrolling), and CoCapture will automatically capture the Document Object Model (DOM) changes. (Step 2) In CoCapture’s
main panel, users can add new behaviors on top of the base scene by demonstration; that is, by directly manipulating any
elements (e.g., drag and drop the red element in the replay and see immediate changes). (Step 3) Users can remix (post-edit,
e.g., change duration) added behaviors to finalize the mockup. (Step 4) Users can refer to the DOM elements or added behaviors
in the textual description using hypertext.

Figure 2: CoCapture’s main panel (after Step 1 in Fig. 1). To create an animation, a user first clicks on an existing DOM element
(b1) (can select multiple by holding Shift key down) from the base scene (B). Once recording starts (A), the user can demonstrate
the desired behaviors by changing the elements’ properties (C) or directly dragging them in the base scene. Once the recording
is finished, the demonstration will be appended to the Animation List (D) with a set of meta operations, such as adjust start/end
time, replay, and preview. The user can write their question (E) and refer to the animations or DOM elements in the scene by
selecting portions of text and clicking the ‘Link to a Reference’ button. Text with references, or hypertext, is in blue with a click
affordance displaying the relevant context (i.e., highlight elements (b1), replay animations (D)). The process of the animation
(inbetweening) will also be displayed (F). The user can also filter the Animation List (D) to only display the animations related
to the selected elements.

Figure 3: For each created animation, CoCapture provides
information that prompts users about the actions they can
take, including creating visual tags and replaying or preview-
ing the animation. It also supports a set of operations to
make the creation process easier and more accurate, includ-
ing a range slider for time adjustment, as well as options for
cloning, changing, or deleting an element.
Position and rotation icon: overlapping circles ending in a filled circle.
Font-size icon: small and large capital A letters.
Visibility icon: an open eye.

Figure 4: There are three steps to create hypertext: (1) se-
lect portions of the text in the question description, (2) click
“Link to a Reference,” and either (3.1) select an element in
the scene or (3.2) check an animation. The hypertext will be
highlighted afterwards.

Figure 5: Screenshots of two of the user study tasks: the Reddit website (left column), and an SVG game (right column). The
screenshots with a red border (a, c) are the existing UIs, whereas the green ones (b, d) are the desired UIs that the participants
were asked to create and describe during the study. The tasks were designed with three goals: realistic, common, and complex.
For the Reddit website task, the issue with the existing UI is that some of the DOM elements are not responsive to window
resizing user input. For the SVG game task, participants need to add new game behaviors such that when the game character
hits the block and the star shape element, the game scene will change dynamically and a new element (the cyan shield shown
in the last image) will be added to the scene.

Figure 6. Box plots of time in seconds, control in coral and CoCapture treatment in cyan. For visual-reference creation, control median is about 110 seconds, with middle half roughly 65–200, while CoCapture median is about 325, with middle half roughly 280–475 and a long upper whisker near 760. For writing text, control median is about 350 seconds, with middle half roughly 315–380, versus CoCapture median about 95, with middle half roughly 60–145. Control has high outliers near 490 seconds for visual references and near 560 and 800 for text. Participants spent more time creating visual references and less time writing with CoCapture; the source reports both differences p<.0001.

structure.title: A Hybrid Crowd-Machine Workflow for Program Synthesis

figure_descriptions.alt:
Fig. 1. Bashon allows users to create Bash commands from natural language.
It uses a hybrid workflow that integrates crowd workers and an AI for program
synthesis. In this example, the user types a command in natural language:
“List files that are modified more than 30 days ago under the css directory” and
Bashon proposes three Bash commands. The user can press ‘Run’ to execute
any of the proposed commands

Fig. 2. System diagram: This diagram plots both the original Tellina (blue) and Bashon’s (green) workflow. In Tellina’s workflow, first, a natural language
query (1) is sent to an automated entity extraction process (2) which outputs a list of entities, their associated types, and the entity extracted query template (3).
Then, the neural network (4) translates the query and the extracted entities into a list of commands (5) that is sent back to the user (6). In Bashon’s workflow,
the natural language queries first go through the original Tellina system, with automated entity extraction (1-5). The results from this are then evaluated by
crowd workers (7). If they are incorrect (8), they then go to crowd workers for entity extraction (9). Commands resulting from this re-extraction process go
back to crowd workers for a final validation step (7), and the results of this are sent back to the end users (10).

Figure 3. Pipeline compares automated Tellina and crowd components. For 50 queries, Tellina entity extraction has 29.00% precision and 22.64% accuracy; crowd extraction has 85.99% precision and 91.99% accuracy (both marked with three asterisks in the source). Extracted entities and templates feed translation, producing candidate commands. Tellina execution filters invalid results, with 60.3% accuracy. A query such as show only .pdf files and the divided file-system outputs then go to crowd validation, which has 77.04% accuracy and returns valid commands.

Fig. 4. User interface of entity extraction task. Crowd workers can add one
entity at a time by typing the entity they recognize in the query to the text
box (1), and then select the type from a drop down list (2).

structure.title: Expresso: Building Responsive Interfaces with Keyframes

figure_descriptions.alt:
Figure 1 presents an illustration of four different keyframes created in Expresso for a sample web page.
Each keyframe is a rectangle of a different shape and size, representing different viewport sizes.
The four keyframes appear as though on an x-axis, sorted by viewport width, with the narrowest keyframe on the left and the widest keyframe on the right.
There is a bi-directional arrow above the set of keyframes with the label 'viewport width', providing a label for the axis. 
The sample web page shown in the keyframes is adapted from the Mozilla website that we used during one of our study tasks.
Each keyframe has the following items: 1) a blue background, 2) the orange FireFox logo, 3) the text 'The new Firefox' in white font, 4) the text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in white font, 5) a green rectangle representing a button, with the text 'Download Firefox' on it in white font, and 6) an illustration of an open laptop with a Firefox browser shown.
Note that the element and viewport widths mentioned below are not to scale; the keyframes are shrunk down for the figure.
Moving from left to right, the keyframes can be described as follows:
The leftmost keyframe is called k_0 and has a width of 722 pixels. The viewport width is narrow compared to its height, and represents the portrait-view viewport on a mobile device. In keyframe k_0, the whole web page has a blue background. The other elements on the page are all horizontally centered and stacked vertically. At the top is the Firefox logo which is medium-sized. Below that is the text 'The new Firefox' in a small font size. Below that is the text 'Fast for good.' in a large font size. Below that is the long line of text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in a very small font size. Below that is the green 'Download Firefox' button. Below that is the laptop illustration which is of medium size and which is at the bottom of the page. Note that the laptop's x-position is 148 pixels.
The next keyframe is called k_1 and has a width of 990 pixels. The viewport width is approximately the same as the viewport height. In keyframe k_1, the UI elements have the same arrangement as in k_0, with all elements horizontally centered and stacked vertically. All elements are the same size as in k_0. Since k_1's viewport is wider, there is more margin to the left and right of elements. Note that the laptop's x-position is 203 pixels.
The next keyframe is called k_2 and has a width of 1000 pixels. The viewport width is wider than the viewport height. In k_2, the page has the same elements as in k_0 and k_1, but a vastly different layout and some elements are different sizes. k_2 has more of a 2-column layout.  In k_2, the blue background only takes up the top half of the page (the lower half of the page is a placeholder gray). The Firefox logo is smaller and is on the far-left edge of the page. The 'The new Firefox' text is of medium font size and appear directly to the right of the Firefox logo. Below the 'The new Firefox' text appears the 'Fast for good' text of large font size. Below that is the long line of text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in a very small font size. Below that is the green button with the text 'Download Firefox'. The text elements and the green button are left-aligned with each other. On the right side of the screen is the laptop, of large size, with equal margin on its left and right sides. Note that the laptop's x-position is 550 pixels.
The next keyframe is called k_3 and has a width of 1200 pixels. The viewport width is much wider than the viewport height. In k_3, the UI elements have the same 2-column arrangement as in k_2. The only difference is that, with the wider page size, the laptop has more margin on its left and right sides. Note that the laptop's x-position is 650 pixels.
As a summary of the layouts, keyframes k_0 and k_1 have all elements horizontally centered and stacked vertically. k_2 and k_3 have the Firefox logo and all text on the left side of the page, and the laptop on the right side of the page.
Each keyframe has a colored-strip beneath it to help in explaining transitions between keyframes. k_0 has a light green strip, k_1 has a magenta strip, k_2 has a turquoise strip, and k_3 has a brown strip.
Each strip also has a label of the laptop's x-position on it, as the transitions highlighted in this figure are those for the laptop x-position.
There is a colored-strip between each pair of adjacent keyframes representing the transition type.
The colored-strip between k_0 and k_1 is a left-to-right gradient of light green to magenta, indicating a smooth transition between k_0 and k_1.
Similarly, the colored-strip between k_2 and k_3 is a left-to-right gradient, of turquoise to light brown, indicating a smooth transition between k_2 and k_3.
The colored-strip between k_1 (magenta) and k_2 (turquoise) is a solid color of magent indicating a jump transition between k_1 and k_2. Specifically, the magenta color means that the range between k_1 and k_2, namely viewport sizes 991 to 999 pixels, should continue the behavior for the laptop x-position from the smaller viewports. This means that the laptop (and all UI elements) are shown horizontally centered and stacked vertically for the range of viewports 991 to 999 pixels wide.
There are range arrows below the set of keyframes indicating the laptop x-position. For the range of viewports less than 1000 pixels wide, there is an arrow pointing left with the label 'laptop is centered in viewport' beneath it. For the range of viewports greater than or equal to 1000 pixels wide, there is an arrow pointing right with the label 'laptop is on the right side of the viewport'.

Figure 2 presents an illustration of the Expresso user interface.
In this illustration, the sample web page used is meant to look like a shoe catalog on a shopping site, and is adapted from the Bass website.
On the left side of the figure is part 'a', which is the web page viewing area.
For this example, the viewing area contains the shoe catalog website, containing the following elements: 1) a brown rectangle at the top representing the page header, with the 'Bass' logo centered, 2) on the left side, a list of menu items with text 'WEEJUNS', 'WOMEN', 'MEN', 'KIDS', 3) a tall and thin brown rectangle representing the border of the left menu bar, 4) in the body of the web page, six Bass loafer shoes arranged in 2 rows of 3; from left to right, the top row contains light green, red, and yellow shoes; from left to right, the bottom row contains pink, lilac, and brown shoes, 5) the pink shoe is currently in 'selected' mode, where it has a black border around it.
At the bottom of the figure is part 'b', which is the keyframe menu.
It contains a list of keyframes for the current responsive web page, represented in a list from left to right with 'width' and 'height' viewport sizes.
For this particular example, the keyframe sizes are, from left to right, 1) width 635 pixels and height 752 pixels, 2) width 769 pixels and height 752 pixels, 3) width 780 pixels and height 752 pixels, and 4) width 1200 pixels and height 752 pixels.
Currently the keyframe of width 780 pixels is selected, which is indicated by its tab having a blue background; the web page shown in the viewing area in the illustration is this keyframe of width 780 pixels.
To the right of the keyframe list, the bottom part of the figure also has a button with the label 'Result webpage (click to resize)' which users can click in order to enter 'resize' mode.
To the right of this are 'Create new keyframe' and 'Delete current keyframe' buttons.
On the right side of the figure is part 'c', which is the element property values menu.
This menu appears in the format of a table and contains the current property and transition values for the currently selected UI element in the viewing area, in this case, the pink shoe.
On the left side of the table are the property values, with the properties 'width', 'height', 'x', and 'y' in the first column, and the corresponding values '183px', '183px', '157px', and '378px' in the second column.
On the right side of the table are the transition rules for each element property.
For each element property, there are dropdown menus for setting transitions between keyframes.
From left to right, the elements are: 1) the 'Left' label with a magenta background, 2) a dropdown widget with colors magenta, turquoise, and magenta-to-turquoise gradient, 3) the 'Current' label with a turquoise background, 4) a dropdown widget with colors turquoise, orange, and turquoise-to-orange, and 5) the 'Right' label with an orange background.
For this example, all four properties for the currently selected item have the following transition settings: the dropdown widget between 'Left' and 'Current' is magenta, indicating a jump transition; and the dropdown widget between 'Current' and 'Right' is the turquoise-to-orange gradient, indication a smooth transition.
To illustrate the different options in the dropdown widget, the second row dropdown between 'Left' and 'Current' is open.

Three graphs compare transition rules between the Left keyframe (magenta) and Current keyframe (turquoise), with viewport width on the horizontal axis and property value on the vertical axis. The left graph has a magenta-to-turquoise gradient selector and a rising straight line connecting the two solid keyframe points: values interpolate smoothly. The middle graph has a solid magenta selector: a horizontal magenta line continues the value from the Left point up to an open circle at the Current viewport width, where the higher solid Current point causes a jump. The right graph has a solid turquoise selector: a horizontal turquoise line extends backward from the Current point to an open circle at the Left viewport width, immediately above the lower solid Left point. Dashed horizontal lines show the continued behavior outside the interval. Thus the gradient interpolates, solid magenta continues the behavior from smaller widths, and solid turquoise continues the behavior from larger widths.

structure.title: Adasa: A Conversational In-Vehicle Digital Assistant for Advanced Driver Assistance Features

figure_descriptions.alt:
Figure 1: (A) The proposed digital assistant, Adasa, identifies user’s questions or commands regarding ADAS features in human
language and responds with answers or actions accordingly. (B) Adasa is integrated into a commercially available vehicle for
evaluation and a real-world driving user study. (C) Adasa is able to access vehicle CAN signals via Bluetooth to conduct system
diagnosis or system control. (D) Adasa setup, driver enables Adasa by pressing the button on the wheel to start the conversation.

Figure 2: Overview of Adasa system, which is designed based on recent publications [20] and integrated with a commercially
available vehicle [8]. Driver’s voice captured by the microphone is translated into its text equivalent ( 1 ) and is passed to Query
Classifier to identify the type of query ( 2 ). Execution Logic operates the query ( 3 ) and retrieves the information needed from
either Knowledge Base ( 4 ) or the vehicle ( 5 ) depends on the type of query. Vehicle-data Ingestor receives the CAN data through
the vehicle interface and records the status of each signal in Vehicle State Repository ( 6 - 7 ). Once the result is passed back to
Execution Logic ( 8 ), the response is converted to a WAV file and output to the speaker to answer driver’s questions ( 9 - 10 ).

Figure 3: An Amazon MTurk task assignment example. We
asked the MTurk workers to rephrase the statement, “what
does it mean if I see a red line and a grey line on the dash-
board?” with the picture of the entire dashboard and a red
bounding box around the area of inquiry in order to help the
workers understand the questions and task at hand.

Figure 4. The driving-study route is shown as a blue loop around northeastern Ann Arbor, starting and ending near the University of Michigan North Campus. Numbered red markers 1–8 identify route segments around the loop. The 11.7-mile route combines 7 miles of highway and 4.7 miles of suburban roads to support testing adaptive cruise control and lane keeping.

Figure 5. Mean questionnaire scores on a 0–10 scale, with error bars. System quality: Q1 acceptability 9.3, Q2 intelligence 8.0, Q3 understanding features 8.9. Information quality: Q4 usefulness 7.5, Q5 accurate diagnosis 7.4. User satisfaction: Q6 pleasantness 7.8, Q7 nervousness 3.4, Q8 responsiveness and reliability meeting expectations 7.1. The low Q7 value indicates participants generally did not feel nervous; the other means are above 7.

structure.title: Codelets: Linking Interactive Documentation and Example Code in the Editor

figure_descriptions.alt:
Figure 1. Codelets attach helpers to regions of code. Helpers are dis-
played inline with the rest of the code without obscuring it. This Codelet
creates a jQuery Mobile button. Its helper is interactive and allows its
user to customize the button by interacting with a form, drawing a line to 
illustrate which region of code each form element is changing. The user
may also edit the code and the form will automatically update itself.

Figure 2. Our augmented editor allows Codelets to be searched for and inserted in the editor, searching for stored Codelets based on their keywords 
and descriptions. The search box (A) is invoked using a keyboard shortcut. If a result is selected, a Codelet (B) is inserted following the caret.

CSS Rounded Corners Codelet beside a CSS editor. The helper offers an all-corners radius slider and separate controls for the four corners; links connect those controls to highlighted border-radius declarations in the source. Adjusting the helper therefore changes the corresponding CSS values.

Figure 4. This Codelet displays a warning (D) after it detects the ab-
sence of a required library. On its right side (E) is a link to a Codelet for 
including the library. The link can be dragged into place and its Codelet 
(F) is inserted.

Figure 5: grouped bar charts compare the control group in blue with Codelets in red. Mean completion time falls from about 22.2 minutes to 12.7 minutes; mean browser refresh count falls from about 19 to 9. Error bars show variation. Both reductions are statistically significant.

A Codelet displays the warning 'I don’t understand the attached code. May I overwrite it?' above the example-code area. Buttons labeled Overwrite, Don’t and Never let the programmer permit this overwrite, decline it, or disable future overwrites. This appears when the attached code cannot be understood by the helper.

Figure 8. For consistency, Codelets have a standard mechanism for
displaying warnings with text and any number of buttons. Helpers can
take advantage of their semantic understanding of what their attached
example code is supposed to do to display warnings even if the code is
syntactically correct. This Codelet, for reading a file in Java, displays an 
error because the programmer has not specified a filename.

structure.title: Natural Language Search of Structured Documents

figure_descriptions.alt: S equals the ordered sequence s sub 1, s sub 2, through s sub n. The summary S contains n sentences.
E equals the collection e sub 1, e sub 2, through e sub m. E contains m game events.
Basic classifier pipeline. A sentence s and the set of game events E enter a classifier. Its output F is the subset of E described by that sentence; F may be empty.

MLB.com Gameday screenshot used as the source of game events. It shows Boston playing Cleveland, with a central batter-and-pitch display and pitch trajectories, the score and inning across the top, player and field information at left, a line score and batting statistics at right, and a play-by-play panel below. The application exposes pitch speed, movement and outcome along with game statistics.

Screenshot of an unassembled inning XML file. Nested inning, top or bottom half, at-bat and pitch elements store the play-by-play data. Attributes identify the batter, pitcher, balls, strikes, outs and a natural-language play description. Appendix A supplies a native-text example of the combined XML representation.

Screenshot of an unassembled players XML file. Player elements are grouped by away and home team; attributes provide identifiers and names plus game statistics. The system uses these player records to interpret names in summaries. Appendix A provides a native-text sample of the assembled player records.

Boston-perspective newspaper-style game summary, shown as an example of natural-language training text. It describes the same Boston–Cleveland game as the adjacent Cleveland summary; the two summaries select and emphasize different events.

Cleveland-perspective game summary for the same game as the adjacent Boston summary. The differing narrative perspective illustrates why one game can supply several distinct natural-language summaries.

Weka Explorer classifier output. The Classify tab displays the learned J48 decision tree, with indented branches for feature tests and leaf predictions, followed by evaluation statistics and a confusion matrix. Controls at left select the classifier and testing method. This is an example of the tree learned from sentence–event feature pairs; it is not a separate algorithm specification.

One-stage classification pipeline. The sentence and event set are expanded into sentence–event pairs. Simple and generated features are extracted for each pair, and a C4.5 classifier decides whether the event belongs in the set described by the sentence. All candidate pairs, including null events, go through this classifier.

Two-stage classification pipeline. A first feature extractor and C4.5 classifier decide whether the sentence discusses any game event. If its discussed-event set is empty, the output is the empty set. Otherwise the sentence is paired with candidate events, a second feature extractor and classifier evaluate those pairs, and the accepted events form F, the subset of E described by the sentence.

P of w-e given w-f equals P of w-e times P of w-f given w-e divided by P of w-f. The printed expression then equates this to P of w-e times P of w-f given w-e; with w-f fixed, that final relationship is proportionality because the denominator is constant.
Sentence–event score is proportional to P of e times P of s given e.

Translation-like classification pipeline. Each sentence is paired with candidate events. An element-probability model computes P(e), and a sentence-for-element model computes P(s given e). Their product ranks events. A separate result-size predictor, informed by sentence position and part-of-speech analysis, chooses how many highest-ranked events form the final subset F.
Approximate probability of event e: count of events with the same type as e that are discussed by some sentence, divided by count of all events with the same type as e.
Smoothed event probability: one plus the count of discussed events of the same type as e, divided by count of all events of that type plus the number of possible event types.

Named-entity recognition examples. Gary Sheffield, Matsui, Wells, Johnson and Damon are highlighted in blue and labeled Player. New York is highlighted in green and labeled Location; Red Sox is highlighted in red and labeled Team. The annotations separate baseball entities from the surrounding sentence text.

Game-summary excerpt illustrating inning inference. The opening sentence places Johnson in the first inning. Johnny Damon swings through the first pitch; the following sentence describes Edgar Renteria and Manny Ramirez taking strike three, completing a 1-2-3 inning. Those later events inherit the inning established by the opening sentence.

Score sub s,e equals v-pitcher times rho-pitcher, plus v-batter times rho-batter, plus v-other-players times rho-other-players, plus v-stems times rho-stems, plus v-inning-match times rho-inning-match. Each rho is a learned multiplier for the corresponding feature.
P of s given e equals score sub s,e divided by the sum, over all sentences s-i, of score sub s-i,e.
x equals one divided by the number of sentences in S.
x equals two divided by the number of sentences in S.
x equals one.
The number of events discussed by sentence s.

Scatter plot of normalized sentence location from 0 to 1 against the number of game events discussed. Most points lie at zero or one event, fewer at two, and isolated points reach three to six. Sentences in the middle and later part of a summary more often discuss events than opening sentences.

Stacked area chart of predicted sentence context across normalized summary position. The blue Game Events share rises from about one tenth near the beginning to a peak near two fifths around 65 percent of the way through, then declines toward the end. The red Other share fills the remainder. The shape is the fitted context estimate used by the result-size predictor.

Two baseball sentences annotated with part-of-speech and entity tags. Player names and Red Sox are assigned PLAYER and TEAM labels; other words retain grammatical tags such as IN, CD, NN, VBD, AT and TO. The first example begins With two outs, Jay Payton produced an RBI single. These annotations supply the verb-related features for estimating how many events a sentence describes.
The number of events discussed by sentence s.

Horizontal frequency chart of errors in estimating the number of discussed events. Zero error dominates at roughly 420 cases. Errors of plus or minus one occur much less often, and errors with larger magnitude are rare. The chart supports the surrounding statement that estimating result size remains a bottleneck.

structure.title: CodeMend: Assisting Interactive Programming with Bimodal Embedding

figure_descriptions.alt: CodeMend interface. The left editor contains a scatter-plot program and highlights the scatter call. Its output is a colored scatter plot. On the right, the query 'change transparency' produces suggestions for the alpha parameter, with 0.5 highlighted as the current value and alternative values below. Panels A–D identify the editor, plot preview, query box and suggestions.

Figure 2. CodeMend showing a ranked list of suggested functions based
on the query “create a scatter plot”. Clicking on a suggested function
will make the system display a number of images generated by the code
examples using the function.

Figure 3. CodeMend architecture has offline and online stages. Offline indexing gathers code from GitHub and code/text from webpages as training data. Modeling simplifies code representations and trains a bimodal embedding model. Online, a user interacts with a user interface that sends a query and current code context to Ranking and Filtering; the trained model supplies this ranking stage, which returns code suggestions to the interface.

Figure 4. Training pipeline. GitHub and webpages supply code and natural-language content. Code becomes indexed function and argument n-grams; the example simplifies a matplotlib pie chart, title, bounding-box and axis calls. Natural-language content trains an embedding network, supplemented by API docstrings. The combined network takes a code-context vector and a natural-language vector, joins them in a hidden layer and predicts an output code element. In the example, code context plus the words color, set, face, bounding, the, box predict plt.title.set_bbox@1@facecolor, identifier 8206.

Figure 5. Four usage scenarios of the bimodal embedding model, arranged in a two-by-two grid. Each panel shows the same network connecting code context and natural-language input through an intermediate representation to code output; colored nodes and arrows indicate the inputs or outputs used, while unused input branches are gray. Panel (a), Code to Code: code context enters the upper input branch and predicts code at the right. Panel (b), NL to Code: natural language enters the lower input branch and predicts code at the right. Panel (c), NL plus Code to Code: both input branches are supplied to predict code. Panel (d), Code to NL: code context and target code are supplied, with the right-hand arrow pointing into the network and the lower-left arrow pointing outward to indicate natural-language output.

Figure 6. Two-dimensional projection of function-name vectors. Dashed segments connect four pairs: plt.xlim to plt.ylim, plt.xscale to plt.yscale, plt.xticks to plt.yticks, and plt.xlabel to plt.ylabel. In each pair the blue x-related function is left of its red y-related counterpart, with approximately horizontal displacement, illustrating the common x-to-y analogy.

Figure 7. Nested-layer spotlight search expands the pyplot grid function. The function call preview is plt.grid(linestyle="dashed", linewidth=1). Below it, a strip of parameters highlights linestyle, whose explanation says it sets the line style of the line. The next layer lists possible styles, including solid and dashed, allowing the user to refine the function into a parameter value without leaving the editor.

Figure 8. Before-and-after bar-chart pair used to elicit natural-language editing requests. Both plots show Adam, Bobby and Charlie with the same Case 1 and Case 2 bar heights. Plot A uses solid red and blue bars, a grid and a legend to the right. Plot B removes the grid, changes the bars to light salmon and pale blue with diagonal hatching, and moves the legend below the plot.

NEAR_APPROACH of c is the subset PC of correct past code, with n vec sim elements, that maximizes the sum over p in PC of vec_sim of c and p.
y_position of c equals the sum over p sub n in NEAR_APPROACH of c of y tilde sub n multiplied by the softmax weight of vec_sim of c and p sub n cubed.
edit_distance of c sub 1 and c sub 2 equals the Levenshtein distance between norm of c sub 1 and norm of c sub 2, divided by the larger length of those two normalized code strings.

structure.title: Simulating Human Cursor Trajectories for Path-Sensitive GUI Evaluation

figure_descriptions.alt: Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license logo.

Equation 1. J star is the minimum over the lateral offset function d of s of J smooth of d plus J length of d plus lambda bias. Subject to d of zero equals zero, d of L equals zero, and the absolute value of d of s is at most W.

Equation 2. J star minimizes the sum, from k equals zero to N minus one, of smoothness, progress, tracking, and corridor costs. The smoothness cost takes control u sub k; the other costs take next state x sub k plus one. Optimization variables are controls u from zero to N minus one and states x from one to N. Constraints: x sub k plus one equals f of x sub k and u sub k; the initial state x sub zero is given; u sub k belongs to the admissible control set U, and x sub k belongs to the admissible state set X.

Figure 1. Four panels compare simulated and human cursor motion through sine-wave and square-wave tunnels. Orange simulated speed repeatedly rises and falls in the sine tunnel, broadly matching the blue human speed trend. In the square tunnel, the blue human speed has higher, sharper peaks while simulated speed is lower and smoother. Both simulated and human trajectories follow the tunnel shapes; the square-turn paths round the corners. Shaded bands show variability.

Figure 2. Three cascading-menu examples compare human and simulated cursor trajectories from a green starting point to a red target in a submenu. The highlighted orange and blue paths bend diagonally between the menus; the submenu target height increases across the examples. Both path sets show similar curved routes through the menu corridor.

Figure 3. Three icon-grid examples show lasso selection of green target icons among gray distractors. Highlighted human and simulated paths loop around the target clusters while avoiding neighboring icons. The paths bend around different target shapes and remain close to the target boundaries.
